Messages.Body:
So there I was, reading rec.games.trading-cards.jyhad for the first
time in months (after getting my long lost net access restored) and all
I found was a rules question from a newbie, a posting of a deck which
used an obvious strategy and had a poor crypt, which no one had
responded to and a long thread about CL vs. NCL which contained every
single one of the arguments, on both sides, which everyone always uses
during such debates, and which in the history of the universe have
changed the minds of about five people, total.
Frankly, I have no interest in reading this sort of stuff. In an ideal
world, I would be able to use this group as a forum for discussing
tournament-level play with other good players, preferable come who
aren't in my local playgroup, as I see them every week anyway.
Is there anyone else out there interested in this? Please, feel free
to respond with anything that fits my general criterion. Argue about
the tournament metagame. Post an inventive deck (one that has a shot in
competetive play and is in some substantial way new and different). Any
thoughts? Anybody? Anybody? Bueller?
This post seems to have come off a lot more bitter and angry than I
intended. Oh well. I just want to stimulate some good discussion here
that could actually improve my enjoyment of the game. Hope at least one
of you out there is like-minded enough to post a response.

-Steve Wampler-

I played another version of that weenie dominate deck a couple of weeks
ago. I got into the final but really worked hard to get there. I had
to do a lot of table talk and ruthless manipulation of new players. In
fact, I even stooped to being friendly with people and complimenting
their decks. I felt so dirty afterward.

Anyway, the revised design eliminated the wakes and deflections.
Without the entire table ganging-up with omni-directed bleeds, I only
had to worry about my predator's bleeds. And, since my minions would
lose a blood every time I deflected, I decided I'd prefer to take a few
extra bleeds from my predator and keep my minions from hunting. I also
lowered the quantity of Govern bleeds and added more free bleeds. While
lowering my average bleed just a bit, I kept my minions full and
attacking every turn. My three turn bleed totals were higher than what
I was getting with the old Govern focus. I think I finished in third.

My other weenie deck did the weenie obfuscate and night moves dance.
Came in as the first seed and finished second. I ended the weekend as
the highest rated player in L.A. On the other hand, the high-cap decks
won the tournaments. I'd say there is a real parity in the tournaments
right now. It was probably the first time I ever left a tournament
without another clear direction in which to adjust decks for greater
tournament success.

Messages.Author: JediMike
Messages.Body:
I also have not been in this group for a VERY long time. I play every week, have
played in every Crusade:LA since it's inception, and won my fair share. My play
group plays TOURNAMENT STYLE ONLY during game nights as we feel anything less would
be pointless for deck preparation and play technique. Right down to the 2 hour time
limit. I find it hard to believe that serious players would play it any other way.
However, my decks I play on a given game night very greatly than my tourny decks. I
believe tourny decks must be VERY focused and very fast. There's no time for flashy
three card combos that send a Vamp to torpor or Burns it then proceeds to bleed for
a whole 1 pnt of damage. I still can't believe people who play these elaborate
decks and are disappointed when they can't win. I try to keep it very simple, Bleed
big, make it unblockable, and blood manage (by gaining 6 per prey hopefully). Of
course we all know the many debatable way to do all three. Offense IS the best
defense. I love the creative deck Ideas and have many, but save it for the game
group they rarely win a tourney. Of course there is always an exception to the
rule, that's one of the beauties of the game.

It's what I call the "X Factor". Many dedicated players take this for granted. I
find good players showing up to a tournament expecting everyone to be playing on
the same intense level as them. BIG mistake! At least in our tourny there were
several "casual" players and a couple of "newbies" Don't underestimate these
players, they will screw up your game!!! I personally sat predator to a guy I just
taught the game to earlier that morning. He built a deck and to my surprise showed
up to play in a tourny. HE BARLEY KNEW THE GAME! So I licked my chops and prepared
to feast, or so I thought. He intercepted everything I did and did nothing to his
prey. The other decks at the table were light bleed/combat. I was one turn from
ousting my prey when time ran out, the table all got 1/2 VP. It was hell, one guy
took 10 min a turn and the rest of the table wanted to show off 3&4 combo fights
that took forever cause they were slow with there combat. Anyway, my point being we
NEED to be aware that inexperienced players will play in tourneys and won't play
well and wont make plays that we think a blind person should see. It's a side of
the game that's not discussed very often but there are players that play for fun
ONLY on a casual basis and not necessarily to win. Of course we can often steam
roller them too, but that advantage might go to the wrong person at the table also.
If we want new players we have to play with new players and hope we just make it to
the final. The best of the best. Not always there either! It's like the super bowl
some are awesome and some are crappers. I live for the AWESOME INTENSE games that
make your hands sweat and your neck sore from staring at the cards, the perfect
hand of seven, knowing your pray probably has just as good of a hand and all of his
minions are untapped! It makes all worth while!

***JediMike***

One of the things Steve wanted to see was innovative-but-competitive deck
ideas, so i'm reposting my Malkavian OOT Prince-protean combat deck. This is
an updated version, probably fifth edition by now.

The basic idea is to use Madness Network actions to rush OOT and strike for
agg damage, so that you can whack a rotschreck on to Kibosh SCE and damage
prevention decks. Some judgement is required in playing the Rotshrecks since
you have to play them simultaneously with the strikes, and you only get one
Rotshreck per time round the table. Then you use weenies to diablerise [or
you block and diablerise].

It works BRILLIANTLY. At the last Portsmouth tournament there were two decks
like this, and mine got 5 and Rob Treasure's got 12 in the heats. Then we
contested each other to death in the final. It's doubtful whether Rob will
ever speak to me again as a result, but i honestly had no choice - my then
version of the deck ABSOLUTELY relied on Greger Anderssen.

Apart from reducing its reliance on the toothsome Prince of Stockholm, i also
adoapted the deck in view of the fact that William Lee's !Nos "Cailean says
the range is LONG" deck beat me up quite badly in two of the heats there [A
Lasombra Shadow step deck would do the same thing, of course]; so i decided
to put in a bit of LR agg dam. Here roughly is the deck as it currently
stands:

CRYPT:
3 x Greger Anderssen
2 x Whatsisponsyface, Prince of Monaco
2 x Zebulon
Victoria
Watenda
Dollface
Normal
Brazil

4 x Madness Network
7 x Rotshreck
2 x Tribute to the Master
4 x Protean
2 x Fame
The Rack

12 x Bum's Rush
4 x Progeny

4 x Swallowed by the Night
2 x Rapid Change

9 x Second Tradition: Domain
4 x Precognition
2 x Eagles' Sight

2 x Homunculus

Ivory Bow
White Phosphorous grenade

13 x Claws of the Dead
3 x Flesh of marble
6 x Form of the Ghost
2 x Body of Sun

As you see, a VERY focussed combat deck whose [almost incidental] Plan B is
swarm bleed. Rob's deck is similar but not quite so focussed on combat. We
more- or-less evolved the concept independently, i believe, though of course
one talks about decks during tournaments and passes ideas around.

****************************

On a separate topic but in the same thread, and much as it pains me to
disagree with my old friend JediMike [from jol64 - Hiya matey!], i really do
not think you and steve are thinking clearly about the purpose of
tournaments. IMO tournaments are there purely and simply to promote the game.
Thus if they are working properly there should always be a healthy proportion
of new guys n gals coming along and playing, often playing badly and
generally losing of course but ALWAYS being cossetted and aided by the
experienced players.

This is certainly the philosophy at Portsmouth - we experienced players are
RUTHLESS with each other but we give the new people every possible aid short
of actually showing them which cards they should play to oust us. [Actually
come to think of it on the Isle of Wight i near enough did that - two new
people turned up and i lent them two of my decks and showed them how to play
the decks.] So as i see it there are TWO tournament metagames - one is the
jousting of the experienced players with each other, but the much more
important one is the less experienced players BECOMING experienced.

Anyway, i don't mean to come over all pompous and sanctimonious - by all
means let's talk about both, and remember that we were ALL totally shit at
Jyhad once upon a time, until some kind person showed us how to play
properly.

Yeah, this is the problem I was referring to, just had to drastically
over-simplify for the purpose of brevity in my initial post.
I'm under no such constraint here, though...

Combat decks are usually great fun to play, and have the greatest
potential for really off-beat strategies that are as or more effective
than the standard ones. It isn't even that difficult to make a comabt
deck that routinely destoys a minion with each of its vampires every
turn, even against the best decks of other types. The problem at
tournament level is, as you pointed out, one of winning the war after
you have won all the battles. The central issue is the fact that most
combat decks rely on a good offense as their defense. The solution to a
dangerous predator is to deprive him of the vampires he planned to use
to kill you. This, however, makes him unable to defend himself from his
own predator. Why do you care? Because in a tournament setting or
competetive play, every victory point counts, and giving an opponent a
free VP is a losing strategy. But simply attacking the grandpredator
simply moves the problem one step further upstream and exarcebating it
by potentially giving away 2 VPs. The solution is, as you said, to
attack all over the table, making sure that no one can oust anyone else
until you can oust your prey with one point bleeds (because combat decks
can't afford to include bleed modifiers... as a friend of mine once
found out, a handful of GtUs is really weak if you're trying to
torporize someone). This is difficult enough on its own, and if there's
another combat deck, or one or more of your opponents has effective
combat defense, well, it would make you despair of winning a tournament
with a combat deck.
But, of course, with no comabt decks in tournies, everyone takes out
their comabt defense, and the next combat deck to show up kills every
vampire in sight. The Metagame wins again.

The dichotomy noted here is not really a dichotomy. Playing experimental
decks in no way violates the ultimate purpose of the game, which is to win
victory points. In the short run, certain deck ideas may be more risky
than a proven winner strategy, but in the long run, if you are predictable
and lack creativity, you will win fewer games.

Experimentation is essential to the good player. A wise player will, of
course, tend to experiment more when the stakes are low, and be more
conservative when the stakes are high, but the killer deck he uses when
the stakes are higher is quite likely to be the product of experimentation
when the stakes are low. Playing a risky "fun" deck in a friendly game in
no way means you are not playing to win. The same is true for
chess-players who try experimental moves in low-stakes games.

Another reason why it is essential to be unpredictable and "fun" in
friendly games is that everyone knows you. Your "best deck" won't win too
often if everyone knows what to expect. In a tournament, where most
opponents have not played you before, you can pull out what you think to
be your current "best deck" with far fewer qualms.

When you look at the big picture (which goes beyond each single game) then
playing for fun in no way contradicts the notion of playing to win. In
fact, it is people who truly play for motives other than victory that are
regarded as "unsportsmanlike" and tend to spoil the fun for everyone. An
example might be the player whose goal is to oust a specific player,
regardless of whether this helps him gain victory points or not.
